sm: The Franklin Board of Mayor and Aldermen met on November 10, 2026. The roll was called, Alderman Barnhill gave the invocation, and the pledge was recited. The meeting opened with recognition of the 2026 Fire Prevention Week helmet shield design contest, themed on safe charging of lithium-ion devices. Fire staff listed tips: use approved chargers, charge on hard surfaces, unplug when full, watch for overheating or swelling, and charge e-bikes and scooters outside. Each participating grade's first-place winner receives a fifty dollar gift card. The mayor noted the beer board had run long that evening.

Winners were announced for kindergarten through sixth grade, and several families who have supported the contest over the years were recognized. The grand prize went to first grader Aurora Leftwitch, whose artwork appears on Sparky the Fire Dog's helmet at Fire Station 8 in West Haven. She received a plaque and a one hundred dollar gift card. Citizen comments followed. Lance Shelby of Heath Place objected to the proposed year-long closure of Lewisburg Pike, saying it would disrupt 146 households. He noted that 675 daily vehicle trips were deemed too many to accommodate, and he asked who represents the families' interests and what alternatives were evaluated.

Shelby asked the board to require documented evaluation of alternatives, such as controlled resident access during safe construction periods. Jeff Leadbetter, a twelve-year resident, welcomed the coming sidewalk but asked the board to reconsider closing access for a year. Diane Shocki, a 33-year resident, said the sidewalk is only three-tenths of a mile and compared it with other sidewalk projects where roads stayed open. She also raised flooding and how residents would get out. The consent agenda, items 18 through 25, passed unanimously. The board then moved item 16 ahead of item five. The city administrator announced the 25th annual Veterans Day parade at 11 a.m. downtown, with the landfill closed and residential waste and recycling collection delayed a day.

Minutes from the October 27 work session and meeting, and the November 2 special work session, were approved unanimously. The board then approved Resolution 2026-91, adopting a comprehensive Historic Franklin preservation plan. The motion also endorsed retooling the Civil War Historic Commission option, and it passed unanimously. For vice mayor, Alderman Burger nominated Greg Caesar and another alderman nominated Matt Brown. The roll call ended in a tie. The mayor broke it by voting for Alderman Caesar, who became vice mayor, after thanking outgoing Vice Mayor Bagot. The mayor made no committee changes. The beer board appointments of Caesar, Barnhill and Pototts passed, and the pension committee appointments were also approved.

The pension committee appointment passed unanimously. The board then opened the public hearing on Ordinance 2025-9, rezoning 20.33 acres at 318 Franklin Road and Harpeth Industrial Court to a planned district with 187 multifamily units and 75,000 square feet of non-residential space. Staff and the planning commission recommended approval, saying it fits the Factory District concept. Greg Gamble of Kimley-Horn, for the applicant, said the developer will add a vehicular and pedestrian connection to the Factory. Alderman Brown and Vice Mayor Caesar voiced concerns about Franklin Road capacity and left turns out of the development. Alderman Burger asked about a roundabout.

A traffic representative for the applicant said a roundabout was studied but did not work because of too much north-south traffic. Off-site road improvements were set by the city's third-party reviewer. Aldermen debated the roundabout, land cost and who would pay. The applicant offered to defer 30 days. Alderman Pototts moved to defer to the December 8 meeting for more traffic analysis. Alderman Brown asked what it would take to widen Franklin Road toward Mack Hatcher, and Vice Mayor Caesar said the new connection through the Factory parking lot changes the traffic picture and might need more than 30 days.

Aldermen asked what information they want back, including options for Franklin Road and the new connecting lane. The applicant agreed to bring back an option for reaching Mack Hatcher, noting it would be very expensive. Staff said the discussion could be paired with a work session. The deferral passed six to two, with Alderman Barnhill and Alderman Peterson voting no. Item 10, Resolution 2025-51, the development plan for Harpeth Village, was also deferred unanimously to December 8 after the public hearing.

The board held a public hearing on Ordinance 2026-24, rezoning 19.11 acres at Branch Creek Crossing to cut commercial square footage and add residential units. Staff said the plan fits the Neighborhood Mixed-Use concept and recommended approval. Greg Gamble said an office building would be replaced by four three-story buildings with ten condos each. He asked that the emergency connection be allowed either north through the church or south through the office parking lot. Alderman Pototts asked whether any units would be deed-restricted for attainable housing, and the answer was no. The ordinance passed unanimously with the new condition. Staff then presented Resolution 2026-79, a revised development plan for 40 dwelling units, with two modification requests.

Modification standard three, allowing current parking requirements of 2.25 spaces per two-plus-bedroom unit, was approved unanimously. Modification standard four, allowing one architectural attribute instead of two, also passed unanimously. Resolution 2026-79 then passed unanimously with both modifications and the new emergency-access condition. The board approved contract 2026-0373 with BBC Investments for a parkland impact fee and construction agreement. It also approved on first reading Ordinance 2026-28, rezoning 26.85 acres at Huffines Ridge Drive, with a public hearing set for December 8. Ordinance 2026-31, creating CCTV inspection and footage review fees, passed first reading with a hearing on November 24. Change order one with Vulcan Construction Materials for East McEwen Drive Phase 4 added $285,743.66 and passed. The city also learned it received over $385,000 for transit, requiring an $80,000 match, and the meeting adjourned.
